children: Corn for March delivery fell 0.8% Friday on the Chicago Board of Trade to $4.48 3/4 a bushel, closing out a negative week for commodities with losses.
Wheat for March delivery declined 0.5% to $5.92 a bushel.
Soybeans for January delivery rose 1.1% to $12.20 3/4 a bushel.

No Risk Premium: Grains trading is likely to remain choppy in the short term as markets tussle with currency issues, South American weather and changes in global trade flows with no Russia-Ukraine peace deal likely, AgResource said in a note. "ARC maintains there's little to no risk premium in grains markets currently, and the assumption is that geopolitics and South American weather progress smoothly through the balance of 2026," the firm said. They also added that it won't take much in the way of shifting grain flows or weather scares in South America to give prices a boost.

Forecast Tweak: The International Grains Council raised its 2026/27 global production estimate for wheat and coarse grains by 1 million metric tons to 2.428 billion tons, with higher wheat and barley numbers offsetting lower corn. The biggest changes were increases for Turkey, Australia and Argentina, and a reduction for the U.S., the IGC says. Ending grain stocks are raised by 7 million tons to 626 million tons, "inflated by unusually heavy inventories in Russia and Ukraine." Soybean production is seen at 439 million tons, unchanged from the October forecast.
Flash Sale: The USDA reported sales of 100,000 metric tons of soybean cake and meal for delivery to Spain during the 2026/2027 marketing year.

Bears vs. Bulls: Corn futures typically rise between Thanksgiving and year-end, with the March contract making an average gain of 32 cents a bushel between Nov. 20 and Dec. 31 in the past 12 years, Naomi Blohm of Total Farm Marketing said in a note.

"The old expression for grains: 'the bears get Thanksgiving, but the bulls get Christmas' may have rung true with the lower price action this November," she said. While each year has its own fundamental supply and demand perspectives, the March contract has had some sort of rally during the period since 2014. Some lasted only days, but others stretched to weeks.

Looking Up: Citi Research maintains a positive view on a number of agricultural commodities including corn and soybeans, and sees the recent drawdown as a buying opportunity. "We still expect El Niño to have larger impact on yields in the next 3-6 months," global head of commodities research Max Layton said in a note. Markets will also start taking notice of the Black Sea closure as Ukraine typically ramps up exports during this time of year. "Exports of both corn and soy have been relatively strong and we expect China delivering on their commitments on buying U.S. soy and potentially corn," Layton added.
The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
The USDA will release its weekly Crop Progress report at 4 p.m. ET Monday.
The USDA will release its monthly Cold Storage report at 3 p.m. ET Tuesday .
The EIA will release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update report at 10:30 a.m. Wednesday
